title: Entanglement from particle number fluctuations in a second-order topological insulator
abstract: Higher-order topological insulators are materials with a bulk energy gap featuring gapless modes at $(d-n)$-dimensional edges, where $n > 1$. Despite this modified bulk-boundary correspondence, their nontrivial topology can nevertheless be observed through the bipartite entanglement spectrum. Inspired by works suggesting fluctuations in conserved quantities could be used to study topology in one-dimensional systems, which likewise feature zero-dimensional edge modes, we extend this treatment to a two-dimensional second-order topological insulator where corner states play an analogous role. We show that the standard bipartite entanglement entropy and particle number fluctuation lack striking signals of topological phase transitions, both in the static case and in the time evolution after a quench, obscured by an area-law term from the subsystem edges. By introducing a quadripartite construction of the subsystem, we show that it is possible to isolate the topological contributions, producing sharp transition peaks in both quantities, observable by studying subsystems much smaller than the full system. As particle number fluctuations are accessible in existing experiments, these results establish a concrete and scalable path to experimental detection of the entanglement in higher-order topological insulators.
summary: This paper develops a novel theoretical method to detect topological phase transitions in higher-order topological insulators using particle number fluctuations. By employing a sophisticated quadripartite subtraction scheme, the authors successfully filter out trivial boundary noise that obscures the signal in standard entanglement measures. This establishes a scalable, experimentally relevant pathway for characterizing topological materials.
main_problem: To find experimentally accessible quantities, like particle number fluctuations, that can reveal the topological phase transitions in higher-order topological insulators (HOTIs).
main_result: Standard entanglement entropy and particle number fluctuations fail to show sharp topological signals due to boundary contributions, but a quadripartite construction successfully isolates these signals, revealing clear transition peaks.
method: The authors employ advanced subtraction schemes (quadripartite construction) applied to both entanglement entropy and particle number variance to filter out trivial boundary effects.
model_or_system: The study focuses on a two-dimensional second-order topological insulator, modeled by a specific Hamiltonian involving hopping and mass terms in orbital and spin space.
key_observables: Bipartite entanglement entropy ($S_{vN}$), particle number fluctuation variance ($	ext{Var}N$), and their topologically corrected versions ($\Delta S, \Delta F$).
important_parameters: The mass parameter $m$ controls the topological phase transition, and the analysis considers both static and time-evolution (quench) regimes.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the topological contribution can be isolated by subtracting the contributions from smaller, non-topological subsystems (quadripartite construction).
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the failure of raw entanglement/fluctuation measures to show transitions, contrasted with figures showing sharp peaks in the corrected quantities ($\Delta S, \Delta F$) at the critical points.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical system and the failure of standard measures. It then introduces the quadripartite subtraction scheme to derive corrected observables, demonstrating the clear topological signatures in both static and dynamic measurements.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, measurable diagnostic tool ($\Delta F$) for detecting topological order in condensed matter systems, which is highly relevant for experimental condensed matter theorists.

This corresponds to making use of the reduced density matrix. (b) Energy spectrum of the model used here as a function of the parameter m for a system size L = 30. At m = ±2 the gap closes signifying a transition to a second-order topological insulator when |m| < 2. The eigenvalues have been colored by the inverse participation ratio IPR = P

FIG. 3. Schematic of the partition of the subsystem used for obtaining entanglement quantities with trivial boundary contributions removed. An initial bipartition into Ωand ¯Ωis defined, and Ωis then further split into a quadripartition as shown.

(a) Modified fluctuations ∆F = VarNAB +VarNAD − VarNAC + VarNC −VarNABD for the setup in Fig. 3 as a function of m, with system size L = 30 and three different subsystem sizes (LΩ= 14, 22, 28) shown.
